idea.body: A fraction names a part of a whole. In 3/4, the bottom number, 4, says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The top number, 3, says how many of those parts you have. A fraction is also a division hiding in plain sight: 3/4 is exactly what you get from 3 divided by 4. If 3 pizzas are shared equally among 4 kitchen stations, each station gets 3/4 of a pizza. A unit fraction, like 1/5, always has 1 on top, one single equal part. When the top number is bigger than the bottom, like 7/4, the fraction is worth more than one whole.

figure.alt: A bar cut into 4 equal pieces with 3 shaded, showing the fraction 3/4.

workedExample.prompt: 5 sandwiches are shared equally among 2 robots. How much does each robot get?
steps: Sharing equally among 2 means dividing by 2: 5 divided by 2.
5 divided by 2 is the fraction 5/2, an improper fraction since 5 is bigger than 2.
5/2 is more than one whole: 2 whole sandwiches use up 4 of the 5, leaving 1 sandwich still to split in half.
So each robot gets 5/2, the same amount as 2 and 1/2 sandwiches.

figure.alt: Two full bars of 2 pieces each shaded whole, plus a third bar of 2 pieces with 1 shaded, showing 2 and 1 half.

ways.name: Share and write as division
ways.when: Use this when more items are shared equally than the number of people sharing.
steps: Sharing equally among 2 means dividing by 2: 5 divided by 2.
Write that division directly as a fraction: 5/2.
5/2 is bigger than 1 whole, since 5 is bigger than 2.
2 whole sandwiches use 4 of the 5 parts, leaving 1 more to split in half.
ways.trap: Writing the fraction upside down, as 2/5 instead of 5/2.

figure.alt: Two full bars of 2 pieces each shaded whole, plus a third bar of 2 pieces with 1 shaded, showing 2 and 1 half.

frames.caption: Write the division as a fraction: 5/2.

ways.name: Cut the whole and count the parts
ways.when: Use this when you can draw the whole cut into equal pieces.
steps: The bottom number is how many equal parts the whole is cut into: 4 stations, so cut the picture into 4 parts.
The top number is how many of those parts you have: 3 out of 4.
Shade 3 of the 4 equal parts on the picture.
The shaded picture shows 3/4, the fraction of a pizza each station gets.
ways.example: 3 pizzas shared equally among 4 kitchen stations
ways.trap: Cutting the picture into pieces that are not all the same size.

figure.alt: A bar cut into 4 equal pieces with 3 shaded, showing the fraction 3/4.

frames.caption: Cut the whole into 4 equal parts.

ways.name: Build from unit fraction pieces
ways.when: Use this when a fraction with a big top number is hard to picture all at once.
steps: Cut one whole into 6 equal slices; each single slice is the unit fraction 1/6.
4/6 means 4 copies of that one slice added together.
1/6 plus 1/6 plus 1/6 plus 1/6 equals 4/6.
Counting 4 unit slices gives the same amount as the fraction 4/6.
ways.example: Build the fraction 4/6 from single slices
ways.trap: Forgetting all the slices must be the same size before counting them.

ways.name: Place it on a number line
ways.when: Use this when comparing a fraction to whole numbers matters more than seeing pieces of one whole.
steps: Mark 0, 1 and 2 as whole numbers on the line.
Cut the gap between each pair of whole numbers into 4 equal parts, since the bottom number is 4.
Count 7 of those quarter-size steps starting from 0.
7 quarter steps land between 1 and 2, exactly 3 quarters past 1.
ways.example: Place 7/4 on a number line from 0 to 2
ways.trap: Cutting only the first whole-number gap into fourths and forgetting to continue the same spacing past 1.

figure.alt: A number line from 0 to 2 marked in quarters, with a dot at 7/4 between 1 and 2.

frames.caption: Cut each gap into 4 equal parts.

bank.prompt: If a shape is divided into 6 equal parts and all 6 are shaded, that equals the whole shape, or 1 whole.
explanation: 6/6 means every one of the 6 equal parts is shaded.
Taking every part of a whole gives you the entire whole.
So shading all 6 parts equals 1 whole shape.
bank.useAgain: when checking that shading every equal part of a shape really does equal the whole thing.
hints: Think about what happens when none of the equal parts are left unshaded.
Compare this to the earlier idea that 3/3 equals 1 whole.
bank.socraticHint: If nothing is left unshaded, how much of the shape is left uncounted?

variant.prompt: If a shape is divided into 9 equal parts and 8 are shaded, that equals more than 1 whole.

bank.prompt: 9 sandwiches are shared equally among 4 friends. How many sandwiches does each friend get? Give your answer as a mixed number.

explanationFigure.alt: Two full bars of 4 pieces shaded whole, plus a third bar with 1 of 4 pieces shaded.

explanation: 9 divided by 4 is the improper fraction 9/4.
4 fits into 9 two whole times, using 8, with 1 left over.
So each friend gets 2 whole sandwiches plus 1/4 more, written 2 1/4.
bank.useAgain: when a sharing problem's answer needs to be given as a mixed number instead of an improper fraction.
hints: Divide the total by the number of friends to get an improper fraction first.
Convert that improper fraction into a whole number part and a leftover fraction part.
bank.socraticHint: After finding how many whole sandwiches each friend gets, what fraction of one more sandwich is left over?

variant.prompt: 11 wraps are shared equally among 4 friends. How many wraps does each friend get? Give your answer as a mixed number.

explanationFigure.alt: Two full bars of 4 pieces shaded whole, plus a third bar with 3 of 4 pieces shaded.

bank.prompt: A rope 13 meters long is cut into 5 equal pieces. How long is each piece, as a mixed number of meters?
explanation: 13 divided by 5 is the improper fraction 13/5.
5 fits into 13 two whole times, using 10, with 3 left over.
So each piece is 2 whole meters plus 3/5 more, written 2 3/5.
bank.useAgain: when a measured length is split into equal pieces and the leftover amount is a fraction of a meter.
hints: Divide the total length by the number of pieces to get an improper fraction first.
Convert that improper fraction into a whole number and a leftover fraction.
bank.socraticHint: How many whole meters fit into each piece before any leftover fraction is needed?

variant.prompt: A rope 17 meters long is cut into 6 equal pieces. How long is each piece, as a mixed number of meters?

bank.prompt: Which situation matches the fraction 5/8?
options: 5 slices shaded out of 8 equal slices
8 slices shaded out of 5 equal slices
5 whole pizzas split equally among 8 friends, how much each friend gets
both the first and third situations describe 5/8
explanation: 5 slices shaded out of 8 equal slices is exactly 5/8, the parts-of-a-whole meaning.
5 pizzas split among 8 friends is 5 divided by 8, which is also exactly 5/8, the division meaning.
Both situations describe the same fraction, just using two different meanings of what a fraction is.
8 slices shaded out of 5 slices is not even possible, since you cannot shade more slices than exist.
bank.useAgain: when a single fraction can be described by more than one real situation, since parts-of-a-whole and division give the same value.
hints: Check each situation by working out what number it actually represents.
More than one of the situations might land on the very same value.
bank.socraticHint: Do the first and third situations both come out to the exact same value, even though they describe different things?

variant.prompt: Which situation matches the fraction 3/7?
options: 3 slices shaded out of 7 equal slices
7 slices shaded out of 3 equal slices
both the first and third situations describe 3/7
3 whole pizzas split equally among 7 friends, how much each friend gets

bank.prompt: 3/5 means the same amount whether it comes from 3 shaded parts out of 5, or from sharing 3 items equally among 5 people.
explanation: 3 shaded parts out of 5 equal parts is the parts-of-a-whole meaning of 3/5.
Sharing 3 items equally among 5 people is 3 divided by 5, the division meaning of 3/5.
Both meanings land on the exact same value, 3/5, just reached in different ways.
bank.useAgain: when checking that a fraction's parts-of-a-whole meaning and its division meaning always agree.
hints: Work out both situations as their own separate calculations.
Compare the two final values.
bank.socraticHint: A fraction has more than one story that leads to it. Do those different stories ever disagree on the final value?

variant.prompt: 1/2 means the same amount whether it comes from 1 shaded part out of 2, or from sharing 1 item equally between 2 people.

bank.prompt: A rover collects 132 rock samples, and 47 of them are red. What fraction of the samples are red?
explanation: The whole collection has 132 samples, so 132 is the bottom number.
47 of the samples are red, so 47 is the top number.
47/132 of the samples are red.
bank.useAgain: when a fraction of a group involves large, less familiar numbers.
hints: The total count is always the bottom number, no matter how large.
The count with the trait you want is always the top number.
bank.socraticHint: Does the size of the numbers change how you find the fraction, or only how big the numbers look?

variant.prompt: A rover collects 210 soil samples, and 68 of them contain ice. What fraction of the samples contain ice?

bank.prompt: A workshop packs 9 boxes with 7 gears each. If 4 gears are used from just ONE box, what fraction of the gears in that ONE box were used?
explanation: The question asks about just one box, not the whole shipment.
One box holds 7 gears, so 7 is the bottom number for that box.
4 gears used out of that box's 7 is 4/7.
bank.useAgain: when a fraction question is really about just one part of a bigger group, not the whole group.
hints: Read carefully which whole the question is asking about: one box, or all the boxes together.
Use only the total from that one box as the bottom number.
bank.socraticHint: Is the 'whole' in this question one box of gears, or every box together?

variant.prompt: A workshop packs 8 crates with 5 tools each. If 3 tools are used from just ONE crate, what fraction of the tools in that ONE crate were used?

bank.prompt: A workshop packs 9 boxes with 7 gears each. If 4 gears total are used from the WHOLE shipment, what fraction of the entire shipment's gears were used?
explanation: The whole shipment has 9 boxes of 7 gears each, which is 9 x 7, or 63 gears in total.
4 gears used out of the entire 63 is 4/63.
4/7 mistakes just one box for the whole shipment, and 4/9 uses the number of boxes instead of the total gear count.
bank.useAgain: when a fraction question about a whole shipment needs the TOTAL count across every group, not just one group.
hints: Find the total number of gears across every box first, by multiplying.
Use that grand total as the bottom number, not the count from just one box.
bank.socraticHint: How many gears are in the entire shipment, across all 9 boxes together?

variant.prompt: A workshop packs 8 crates with 5 tools each. If 3 tools total are used from the WHOLE shipment, what fraction of the entire shipment's tools were used?

bank.prompt: A print run makes 250 sheets, and 84 are damaged. What fraction of the sheets are NOT damaged?
explanation: The whole print run has 250 sheets.
250 minus the 84 damaged sheets leaves 166 sheets that are not damaged.
The fraction not damaged is 166/250, not the fraction that IS damaged.
bank.useAgain: when a question asks for the fraction that is NOT a certain trait, so a subtraction comes before the fraction.
hints: Find how many sheets are not damaged first, by subtracting.
Use that leftover count as the top number, over the total as the bottom number.
bank.socraticHint: Is the fraction not damaged the same as the fraction damaged?

variant.prompt: A print run makes 180 sheets, and 47 are damaged. What fraction of the sheets are NOT damaged?

bank.prompt: In the fraction a/b, if a is bigger than b, the fraction represents more than one whole.
explanation: The fraction equals exactly one whole when the top number equals the bottom number.
If the top number is bigger than the bottom number, there is more than one whole's worth of parts.
So a bigger top number than bottom number always means more than one whole.
bank.useAgain: when deciding whether ANY fraction, not just a specific example, is worth more than one whole.
hints: Think back to when a fraction equals exactly 1 whole.
If the top number grows past that point, what happens to the fraction's value?
bank.socraticHint: You already know a fraction equals 1 whole when its top and bottom numbers match. What happens once the top number passes the bottom number?

variant.prompt: In the fraction a/b, if a is smaller than b, the fraction represents less than one whole.

bank.prompt: 8 identical robots share 3 batteries equally. What fraction of a battery does each robot get?
explanation: Sharing equally among 8 robots means dividing by 8.
3 divided by 8 is the fraction 3/8.
Each robot gets 3/8 of a battery.
bank.useAgain: when the amount being shared is smaller than the number of groups sharing it, giving a fraction less than 1.
hints: Sharing equally always means the total divided by the number of groups.
It is fine for the fraction to be less than 1 whole, since there is not enough for everyone to get a whole battery.
bank.socraticHint: Since there are more robots than batteries, would you expect each robot's share to be more or less than one whole battery?

variant.prompt: 6 identical rovers share 5 solar panels equally. What fraction of a panel does each rover get?

stretch.prompt: A kitchen makes 3 batches of a recipe. Each batch needs 2 and 1/4 cups of flour. How many cups of flour are needed in total, as an improper fraction?
explanation: 2 and 1/4 cups is the same as 9/4 cups, since 2 wholes is 8/4 and 8/4 plus 1/4 is 9/4.
3 batches need 3 times that amount: 3 x 9/4.
3 x 9/4 is 27/4 cups in total.
stretch.useAgain: when a mixed number amount is repeated several times and the total is wanted as one improper fraction.
hints: Convert the mixed number to an improper fraction first.
Multiply that improper fraction by the number of batches.
stretch.socraticHint: Once 2 and 1/4 is rewritten as ninths over 4, what operation combines 3 batches of that amount?

variant.prompt: A workshop uses 1 and 3/5 liters of paint per coat, for 4 coats. How many liters are used in total, as an improper fraction?

stretch.prompt: A print shop uses 5/9 of its paper stock on Monday, and the SAME AMOUNT again on Tuesday. What fraction of the original stock is used in total after both days? It is fine if the answer is more than 1 whole.
explanation: Monday uses 5/9 of the stock, and Tuesday uses another 5/9.
Add the two amounts together: 5/9 plus 5/9 is 10/9.
10/9 is more than one whole stock's worth, since the shop must have restocked between the two days.
stretch.useAgain: when the same fraction is used twice in a row and the total ends up bigger than one whole.
hints: Add the Monday amount and the Tuesday amount together.
It is fine for a total made of fractions to be bigger than 1 whole.
stretch.socraticHint: Does using the same fraction twice always have to add up to less than 1 whole?

variant.prompt: A garden waters 3/8 of its beds on Saturday, and the SAME AMOUNT again on Sunday. What fraction of the beds' worth of watering happens in total? It is fine if the answer is more than 1 whole.

stretch.prompt: A rope 3 meters long is cut into pieces that are each 3/4 of a meter. How many whole pieces can be cut, and is any rope left over?
explanation: Check by multiplying: 4 pieces of 3/4 meter each is 4 x 3/4, which is 12/4, exactly 3 meters.
Since 4 pieces use up exactly 3 meters, nothing is left over.
3 pieces would only use 3 x 3/4, which is 9/4, or 2 and 1/4 meters, leaving too much rope unused.
stretch.useAgain: when checking how many equal fractional pieces fit exactly into a whole-number total, by multiplying back up.
hints: Try multiplying different piece counts by 3/4 to see which one lands exactly on 3.
A piece count that uses less than 3 meters would leave some rope over.
stretch.socraticHint: If 4 pieces of 3/4 meter use up exactly 3 meters, is there anything left to call leftover?

variant.prompt: A rope 4 meters long is cut into pieces that are each 2/3 of a meter. How many whole pieces can be cut, and is any rope left over?

stretch.prompt: A garden path uses pavers that are each 2/5 of a meter long. If the path is 6 meters long, how many pavers fit exactly, with no gap or overlap?
explanation: Check by multiplying: 15 pavers of 2/5 meter each is 15 x 2/5.
15 x 2/5 is 30/5, which is exactly 6.
So 15 pavers fit exactly into the 6 meter path.
stretch.useAgain: when a whole-number length is filled exactly by a whole number of equal fractional pieces.
hints: Try multiplying a guessed number of pavers by 2/5 to see if it lands exactly on 6.
The pavers needed will be more than 6, since each one is less than a full meter.
stretch.socraticHint: Since each paver covers less than a whole meter, would you expect to need more or fewer than 6 pavers to cover 6 meters?

variant.prompt: A print shop cuts ribbon into pieces that are each 3/7 of a meter. If the ribbon is 9 meters long, how many pieces fit exactly, with no leftover?

stretch.prompt: Two different fractions, like 2/4 and 3/6, can represent the exact same amount even though their numerators and denominators are both different.
explanation: 2/4 means 2 shaded parts out of 4 equal parts, which is exactly half.
3/6 means 3 shaded parts out of 6 equal parts, which is also exactly half.
Even though the two fractions look different, they represent the same amount.
stretch.useAgain: when two fractions that look completely different still turn out to represent the same amount.
hints: Work out what fraction of a whole each one actually represents.
Compare the two amounts, not just the numbers written.
stretch.socraticHint: Do 2/4 and 3/6 both simplify down to the same familiar amount?

variant.prompt: Two different fractions, like 1/3 and 2/6, can represent the exact same amount even though their numerators and denominators are both different.
